newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - March 12.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - March 12.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Wednesday:

* The expansion of the U.S. economy is six years old this month and displaying a resilience not shown in earlier periods of sustained growth. Unemployment remains low, consumer spending is strong and industrial production is on the upswing. Yet none of this has led to the shortages and inflation that prompted the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates during past expansions.

* The Securities and Exchange Commission has sharply rebuked the Philadelphia Stock Exchange after two recent scandals involving members of the exchange's board. In an unusual visit to Philadelphia, SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt accused the board of spending more time fighting among themselves than overseeing their regulatory responsibilties.

* Club Mediterranee is hoping to turn around its financial fortunes with the appointment of Philippe Bourguignon, the former head of Euro Disney, as its new chief executive and the hiring other company outsiders.
* A struggle for dominance between the four men who controlled DFS Group Ltd preceeded the sale of the duty free empire to LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton.
* The Dow industrials edged up 5.77 points to close at a record 7,085.16, but the Standard & Poor's 500 stock index and the Nasdaq composite both fell.
* The yield on the 30-year Treasury rose to 6.85 percent.
* The U.S. Labor Department said productivity rose seven-tenths of one percent last year, the largest rise in four years.
* Federal officials arrested Philip John Milligan, the head of a small Manhattan stock brokerage firm, on charges that he accepted a $100,000 bribe to sell worthless stock.
* A Federal grand jury indicted two executives of the Atlanta-based Coca-Cola Bottling Co on charges they bribed a worker to help undermine a unionization campaign in 1994.
* K-III Communications put several properties up for sale, including New Women magazine and The Daily Racing Forum, in a move to shed non-core operations.

* Intel has been embarrassed by a flood of angry elecronic mail responses after it threatened to withdraw advertising from two German magazines that gave unfavorable reviews of a new Intel chip that is not yet on the market.
* The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund may soon forgive up to $300 million in loans they have made to Uganda, which is one of about 20 poor nations that may have their debts forgiven.
* The U.S. Labor Department revealed new rules to protect farm workers by making it harder for farmers to avoid liability for contactors' violations of laws protecting wages and sanitation.

* A number of sites around the world are the destinations of revelers prepared to celebrate on the eve of the year 2000, but a survey finds that Americans' favorite choice is New York City's Times Square.
* Levi Strauss has paid $25,000 for a pair of its jeans that dates back to between 1886 and 1902.
